items.lede: On August 27, Omnis Fuel Technologies, LLC and Quantum Pleasants, LLC filed a formal objection to approval of the cash collateral motion (Dkt. 172, related to Dkts. 17 and 50), supported by thirteen exhibits, and the West Virginia Economic Development Authority filed its own independent objection to both the cash collateral motion and the debtor's bidding procedures motion (Dkt. 171).
items.body_md:
On August 27, Omnis Fuel Technologies, LLC and Quantum Pleasants, LLC filed a formal objection to approval of the cash collateral motion (Dkt. 172, related to Dkts. 17 and 50), supported by thirteen exhibits, and the West Virginia Economic Development Authority filed its own independent objection to both the cash collateral motion and the debtor's bidding procedures motion (Dkt. 171). Those two filings — from the plant's former ownership bloc and from the estate's largest creditor — are the most consequential developments to hit the docket since the August 14 dismissal motion (Dkt. 93), and they converge on the September 3 final hearing from opposite directions.

The Omnis Fuel Technologies / Quantum cash collateral objection (Dkt. 172) is the logical extension of the August 14 dismissal motion: if the court should not have authorized the case in the first place, the interim cash collateral order (Dkt. 50) that underwrites the debtor's continued operation and sale process should not be made final. The thirteen-exhibit attachment signals a factual record built to contest both the debtor's authority to use collateral and the adequacy of adequate protection provided to the prepetition secured parties — the same factual battleground as the dismissal motion. Separately, Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum also filed a formal objection and reservation of rights to the bidding procedures motion and the Houlihan retention application (Dkt. 169, related to Dkts. 84 and 86), directly challenging the sale process architecture before it is court-approved. The Pleasants, LLC (debtor) filed its own reservation of rights regarding the bidding procedures motion (Dkt. 173), preserving flexibility to respond to those objections before or at the September 3 hearing.

The WVEDA's objection (Dkt. 171) carries its own weight. 
The authority holds a $50.9 million unsecured loan obligation that matured in June 2026 and remains unpaid
, making it the largest single creditor in the estate and the party with the most at stake in the sale outcome. Its objection to both cash collateral use and the bidding procedures signals that the debtor does not have the uncontested consent of its major economic stakeholder for the sale framework it is trying to put in place by September 3. For WVEDA's recovery, a contested cash collateral order is a material risk: if the court declines to enter a final order on September 3 or imposes materially different terms than the interim, the operating budget and the sale timeline both come under pressure. On the retention side, the U.S. Trustee filed a formal objection to the debtor's application to employ Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer (US) LLP as bankruptcy counsel (Dkt. 175, related to Dkt. 83). A contested retention application for lead bankruptcy counsel — filed by the U.S. Trustee, not a creditor — is substantively important: if the court sustains the objection in whole or in part, it creates disruption in the debtor's professional infrastructure at the worst possible moment, days before the September 3 hearing complex.

The simultaneous filing by Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum of a Reservation of Rights (Dkt. 177) superseding a prior reservation (Dkt. 170, which was withdrawn at Dkt. 176) regarding the ordinary course professionals motion and certain retention applications (Dkts. 77, 81, 85) rounds out a coordinated filing strategy: the former ownership bloc is now on record opposing the cash collateral, the sale process, the investment banker retention, and the professional retention infrastructure simultaneously. Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld LLP's appearance — through pro hac vice admissions for Scott L. Alberino, Sophia N. Bavaro, and Kate Doorley (Dkts. 178–180) alongside the Pleasants, LLC notice of appearance (Dkt. 174) — adds a second major restructuring firm to the debtor's side of the caption. Akin Gump's entry at this stage, less than a week before the final hearing, suggests the debtor is marshaling additional firepower for the September 3 contested hearing rather than anticipating consent. Dkts. 178–180 are procedural, but Akin Gump's substantive role will become clear once a retention application is filed. The next concrete milestone is September 2, when the § 341 Meeting of Creditors convenes at 1:00 p.m. ET via Zoom, followed immediately by the September 3 final hearing at 1:00 p.m. ET on cash collateral, wages, utilities, critical vendor payments, and bidding procedures — now fully contested on multiple fronts.

items.body_md:
On August 26, Oriel Bachar filed the foreign representative's opposition to Skillz Platform Inc.'s Motion to Compel Production of Documents and Witness for Deposition (Dkt. 78, related to Dkt. 73), attaching fifteen exhibits — a substantive filing that frames the entire dispute heading into tomorrow's virtual discovery hearing before Judge Walrath (Dkt. 76, August 28, 10:00 a.m. ET, Courtroom 4). The volume of exhibits — labeled A through O — signals that Papaya's opposition is document-intensive, likely contesting both the adequacy of its prior production and the scope of what Skillz seeks to compel, rather than offering a clean concession on either prong. That posture is consistent with the strategy telegraphed by Dkt. 77 (the amended deposition notice filed August 24): tender a witness to blunt the deposition-witness prong, then fight the document production demands on the merits.

Also filed today (August 27) are a supplement (Dkt. 81) and a related exhibit (Dkt. 84), both bearing today's date and associated — based on the docket sequence and the hearing context — with the August 28 hearing record. The agenda for that hearing was noticed twice: first by Skillz on August 26 (Dkt. 79, related to Dkts. 73–78), then by a second agenda filed today (Dkt. 82). Two agenda filings for the same hearing is mildly unusual and may reflect the supplement (Dkt. 81) requiring an updated hearing agenda, though the substance of what changed is not apparent from the docket captions alone. Dkts. 80 and 83 are certificates of service — procedural and routine, omitted.

The August 28 hearing is now the case's controlling near-term event. Judge Walrath will hear Skillz's motion to compel (Dkt. 73) on a shortened-notice schedule granted by the August 21 order (Dkt. 75), with Papaya's fifteen-exhibit opposition (Dkt. 78) squarely before her. The outcome determines how much of an evidentiary record Skillz can build before the recognition hearing — the proceeding at which Judge Walrath will decide whether to formally recognize the Israeli insolvency proceeding and whether to extend the stay protecting 
Papaya's U.S. assets from collection and enforcement
. 
The underlying judgment requires Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement and approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and costs
, and Skillz's ability to contest recognition on factual grounds depends directly on the breadth of discovery it can obtain now. If Judge Walrath grants the motion to compel in full, Skillz accelerates its evidentiary build; a denial or a narrow grant limits Skillz's factual record at the recognition hearing and correspondingly improves Papaya's position on the stay. The next hard deadline is the 10:00 a.m. ET virtual hearing tomorrow.

items.body_md:
Today, the nonbinding indications of interest deadline expires
 — the first hard gate in the sale process since Judge O'Hagan entered the bidding procedures order on August 17. 
Prospective buyers seeking any portion of the assets had until today to submit nonbinding expressions of interest, with binding qualified bids due September 8.
 The IOI submissions are not filed on the docket and their contents will not be publicly disclosed; what the estate's investment banker receives today will determine whether the September 10 auction is competitive or a formality ceding the assets to stalking-horse Thor CALAP LLC at the floor. 
The prepetition marketing process generated 28 NDAs, seven LOIs, and three additional indications of interest
 before the petition date, so some market interest pre-existed — but 
NDAs and indications of interest fall short of qualified offers, and prospective buyers still have to value these particular sites above the Thor CALAP terms after accounting for development needs, contracts, and closing risk.


On the docket, Dkts. 180–183 (filed August 26) and the unnumbered hearing-rescheduled entry (filed August 27) each carry generic labels — "Document," "Document," "Motion (Generic)," "Document," and "Hearing Rescheduled" — without descriptive text available in public-facing records. The motion at Dkt. 181 is the only filing that could be substantive; without confirmed document text it cannot be classified with precision, and it is noted here as unverified pending the underlying pleading's public availability. The hearing-rescheduled entry is procedurally important to the extent it affects a near-term date, but the affected hearing and its new date are not identifiable from docket metadata alone. Dkts. 185 and 186 are BNC certificates of notice and carry no independent weight. Anyone tracking a specific motion or hearing in this case should pull the underlying documents directly from the court's CM/ECF system or __[Verita Global](https://veritaglobal.net/poolin)__ to confirm the affected event.


Creditors meet remotely tomorrow, August 28, at 9:00 a.m. ET for the Section 341 examination, where they can question company representatives under oath.
 That examination is the next concrete milestone and carries real weight for recovery analysis: it is the first opportunity for the creditor body — including the ~11,700 wallet IOU holders — to question CRO Michael DuFrayne on record regarding the pre-petition fund movements underlying the Chapter 11 trustee motion (Dkt. 103). The qualified bid deadline follows on September 8, 
with the auction set for September 10 at 10:00 a.m. Eastern, at Archer & Greiner's offices in Voorhees, New Jersey, virtually, or at another location designated by the debtors.
 
Sale objections are due September 16 at 5:00 p.m. Eastern, and the sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan is scheduled for September 18 at 11:00 a.m.

items.body_md:
On August 24, the SEC issued Release No. 106177 in an administrative proceeding (File No. 3-22435), extending the deadline to submit a Proposed Plan of Distribution — most likely to August 26, 2027 — after the Division received four public comments on a proposed plan it published for comment on June 29, 2026. 
The Commission published a Notice of Proposed Plan of Distribution on June 29, 2026 under Rule 1103, inviting public comment through July 29, 2026, and received four comments raising various issues before issuing this extension on August 24, 2026.
 The practical consequence for Class 5 claimants is significant: the August 20 deadline the SEC faced — under the Second Extension Order (Release No. 104875, February 20, 2026, File No. 3-22382) — has now been superseded, and the Commission's own published distribution methodology will not be finalized for another year. The relationship between File No. 3-22382 (the prior Tai Mo Shan extension orders) and File No. 3-22435 (Release No. 106177) requires confirmation against the full order text; the operative point for recovery posture is that the __[SEC's enforcement docket](https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/admin/2026/34-106177.pdf)__ reflects a further extension well past August 20, meaning no distribution framework for the $123.1 million Fair Fund will issue in the near term.


The plan, once submitted, must define investor eligibility, loss calculations, claim requirements, and payment procedures; the deadline does not trigger payouts. Coordination with Terraform's separate bankruptcy recovery remains unresolved, and claims in the bankruptcy proceeding do not automatically establish eligibility for this fund.
 For Class 5 holders with overlapping losses in both tracks, this extension compounds timing uncertainty: the bankruptcy wind-down runs through December 31, 2026, but the parallel Fair Fund track — which could affect net recovery on duplicate losses — now trails it by a year or more. The SEC's apparent reason for the further extension is the public comment process: 
the Commission published a Notice of Proposed Plan under Rule 1103, with the comment period closing July 29, 2026, suggesting the four comments received required the Division to rework or respond to the proposed methodology before a final plan can be submitted.


Dkt. 1325, filed today, is a rescheduled hearing notice — procedural and routine, carrying no independent effect on recovery or claim allowance. The authorization motion filed August 19 (Dkt. 1321) remains unresolved on the public record, with no corresponding order yet appearing on the docket. The next fixed milestone is December 31, 2026 — the court-extended wind-down deadline — with the Jump Trading litigation and *Chang v. Terraform Labs Wind Down Trust* adversary proceeding the primary substantive resolution triggers ahead of that date. On the Fair Fund track, the operative question is now whether the SEC's next extension order (Release No. 106177) covers the same File No. 3-22382 proceeding as the prior Tai Mo Shan orders, or a distinct but related administrative matter; confirmation would come from the full order text available at the __[SEC enforcement docket](https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/admin/2026/34-106177.pdf)__.

items.body_md:
On August 25, the district court clerk docketed Dkt. 685 — a second USCA Case Number entry — confirming that the Ninth Circuit has opened at least one additional appellate proceeding arising from the fee appeals filed by Edelson PC / Oppenheim + Zebrak (Dkt. 682, August 18) and Cowan DeBaets Abrahams & Sheppard LLP (Dkt. 683, August 19). Dkt. 684, filed August 21, was the first such notation; the appearance of a second entry four days later strongly suggests the court assigned separate docket numbers to the two appeals rather than immediately consolidating them into a single track. That said, the specific Ninth Circuit case numbers remain unconfirmed from publicly available sources: 
CourtListener's district-court docket for 4:24-cv-05417 was last updated August 23, 2026, and its data is sourced from PACER and RECAP, which may not be current
 — meaning the appellate docket numbers have not yet propagated to any public aggregator this desk can verify. Confirmation will come once the Ninth Circuit clerk's entries appear on PACER or a public index. For analytical purposes, the operative fact is that two separate USCA Case Number notations now sit on the district docket, one per notice of appeal, consistent with the clerk opening two distinct appellate files.

The substantive posture of the fee dispute is unchanged. 
Two firms involved in generating the $1.5 billion copyright settlement appealed to the Ninth Circuit after being cut out of the $101 million attorney fee award, which was restricted to court-approved class counsel Susman Godfrey and Lieff Cabraser Heimann & Bernstein.
 
A week before he retired, Judge Alsup castigated plaintiffs' counsel for improperly requesting $75 million for work done by the two appealing firms and Cowan DeBaets in an initial $300 million fees request.
 Whether each appellant group is challenging only its exclusion from the fee award or also mounting a broader attack on the July 20 final approval order remains unconfirmed on the face of the notices; that question will be answered when opening briefs are filed. The existence of two separate appellate files — rather than a consolidated one — creates a procedural fork: the Ninth Circuit will need to decide, either sua sponte or on motion, whether to consolidate the proceedings. Consolidation is standard where appeals arise from the same underlying order and share common issues, but it is not automatic, and separate scheduling orders could issue in the interim.

For class members, Dkt. 685 closes the opening phase of the appellate record: both fee appellants now have active Ninth Circuit cases, the Effective Date has not arrived, and the disbursement portal remains dormant. Anthropic's payment obligations run independently of the appeals, and no party has moved for a stay. The $450 million first installment (Scheduled Payment 1) falls due September 25, 2026 — four weeks out. The next concrete milestones are: (1) the Ninth Circuit's scheduling orders establishing opening-brief deadlines for each docket, typically issued within weeks of case opening; and (2) any consolidation order, which would determine whether the two appeals proceed on a unified or parallel track and could affect both briefing timelines and the ultimate scope of any panel decision.

items.lede: On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here.
items.body_md:
On August 25, a party filed Dkt. 483 — an Opposition/Response to Motion — the only new docket entry since yesterday's briefing. The motion being opposed is not identified in the docket text as reproduced here. Given the live motions practice in this case, the most plausible target is Google's August 21 Administrative Motion to Consider Whether Cases Should Be Related (Dkt. 478), whose response deadline was set at August 25 — the same date Dkt. 483 was filed. If that is the motion being opposed, the filing reflects a party — most likely the plaintiff class — resisting Google's effort to link this proceeding to one or more related cases. The case-relation motion, if granted, could shift judicial assignment or coordinate discovery and briefing schedules in ways that affect litigation pace and cost for both sides; if denied, each proceeding continues on its own track. Until Dkt. 483's full text is pulled from PACER, the identity of the filing party, the motion it targets, and the arguments advanced remain unverified and are not stated here.

The more consequential open question from yesterday remains unresolved in any available source: the outcome of the Dkt. 482 omnibus order — which adjudicates class certification, Google's sanctions motion, the outstanding intervention motion (Dkt. 468, Lee Child/Andrew Child/Girlcomix), and three motions for miscellaneous relief — has not been reported by any secondary outlet as of this briefing. The full text of Dkt. 482 on PACER is the controlling document. Until it is pulled, the class's shape, the sanctions disposition, and whether the intervenors were admitted remain unverified. The practical consequence is significant: class certification in this case defines the universe of copyright holders who can share in any statutory-damages recovery, and the per-work structure of § 504(c) means that the breadth of the certified class — authors only, publishers included, works defined by training vs. ingestion — directly sets the ceiling on Google's aggregate exposure.

The next concrete milestone is the resolution of the Dkt. 478 case-relation motion, which is now fully briefed with Dkt. 483's opposition and ripe for ruling. No hearing date is visible in the docket text for that motion. On the merits track, the full text of Dkt. 482 — available on PACER at 5:23-cv-03440 — remains the priority pull; it is the document that determines where this case goes from here.

items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.
